explanation: Identified by a multilobed nucleus (typically 3–5 lobes connected by thin chromatin strands) and fine lilac (neutral-staining) cytoplasmic granules. It is the most abundant circulating white blood cell.
A small agranular cell with a large round densely clumped nucleus and only a thin rim of blue cytoplasm. The high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio is the key giveaway.
The largest peripheral blood leukocyte, with a large kidney- or horseshoe-shaped nucleus and gray-blue cytoplasm containing fine dust-like granules, sometimes with vacuoles.
Recognized by its bilobed nucleus and abundant uniform brick-red (orange-red) granules that fill the cytoplasm on a Wright-stained smear. The granules are the identifying feature.
Large dark purple-black coarse granules that often obscure the nucleus. It is the least abundant circulating leukocyte, and the intensely basophilic granules are the identifying feature.
Anucleate biconcave discs with a smooth round outline and a central pallor occupying about one-third of the cell diameter, uniform in size (MCV roughly 80–100 fL).
Spherical cells that retain crystal violet and stain purple, arranged in grape-like clusters — the classic Gram-stain appearance of Staphylococcus (chains would suggest Streptococcus).

Rod-shaped bacteria that lose the crystal violet during decolorization and take up the safranin counterstain, appearing pink-red. The thin peptidoglycan layer with an outer membrane drives this reaction.
Round to oval cells showing narrow-based budding daughter cells without true hyphae; pseudohyphae may accompany them, as commonly seen with Candida species.

Colorless, envelope-shaped crystals (a square with an X across the face) — the classic dihydrate form; the monohydrate form appears as dumbbells or ovals. They are common in acidic urine and are notably seen in ethylene glycol poisoning.

A translucent, colorless cylindrical structure with parallel sides and rounded ends, formed from Tamm-Horsfall protein in the distal nephron; it is best seen with reduced microscope light and contains no inclusions.
Elongated crescent-shaped red cells with pointed ends, caused by polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin S. Irreversibly sickled cells retain the shape even when reoxygenated.
